items.title: Ending The Defender’s Dispatch
items.content_html:
I’m ending The Defender’s Dispatch after 13 issues. Issue 013, published November 9, was the last one.

I started the newsletter to give practical cybersecurity and IT stories more room than a roundup allows. I’m glad I made it, but preparing the web edition and email every week became a source of stress. Some issues went out later than planned, and I don’t want to keep promising a schedule that’s wearing on me.

I wrote a longer note about the decision on the Dispatch page. The full archive will stay online. I’ll keep writing here, including Security Signal Weekly. Thank you to everyone who read, subscribed, or sent a story.

items.title: SonicWall's SAML VPN Bypass: The Questions MSPs Need to Answer
items.content_html:
A ticket that says “SonicWall patched” leaves out the question at the center of CVE-2026-19868: which sign-in routes would the SSL VPN accept, and did they all enforce the intended controls? For an MSP with several client firewalls, that question needs an answer for each deployment, not just a firmware job marked complete.

SonicWall published its SonicOS advisory on November 6. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security says SonicWall has observed exploitation, and CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. That calls for an expedited review. It does not establish that every SonicWall firewall, or every client using one, has been compromised.

The credential condition matters

The published CVE description says a person with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method may be able to bypass SAML authentication controls in the SonicOS SSL VPN service. If MFA is enforced through that SAML route, successful exploitation may bypass that MFA requirement too. The flaw affects the Gen7 and Gen8 SonicOS branches identified in the vendor’s advisory.

Those details set the boundary of the claim. The public description does not say an attacker can connect without any valid credentials. It does show why a configuration labeled “SAML with MFA” is insufficient evidence of protection when another login method is available. The firewall’s actual authentication paths determine what a user can do.

Find the configurations, not just the appliances

Start with the firewalls you manage, then narrow the list by what is reachable and how SSL VPN is configured. For each device, record its model, running SonicOS version, SSL VPN exposure, SAML provider, other enabled login methods, and the owner of the change. A firewall in inventory and an exposed SAML VPN with an alternate credential path are different findings.

Check the current SonicWall advisory against each model and release branch before assigning a fixed build. The Canadian bulletin identifies affected release ranges as of November 6, but the vendor’s current matrix should control the upgrade decision. Record the version you observed on the device and the advisory revision you used. A copied version number with no appliance or branch attached is hard to audit later.

If you establish that an appliance does not use the affected authentication path, record the configuration evidence. If you cannot tell which methods are enabled, leave that client open for investigation. An unverified configuration is not a clean result.

Patch and test the route people actually use

Plan the update as a remote-access change. Back up the configuration through the client’s normal process, agree on a recovery route, and account for the VPN interruption. Avoid leaving an alternate login method enabled for convenience during maintenance without checking what controls it enforces.

After the upgrade, confirm the running firmware version on the appliance. Then use an authorized test account to complete a normal VPN sign-in through the intended SAML provider and MFA flow. Review the sign-in result in both the VPN and identity-provider records. Check the other configured authentication methods against the client’s access policy so a fallback route does not quietly weaken the requirement you just tested.

This is configuration testing during an approved change window, not a reason to run an exploit against a production client firewall. Where you cannot safely test a path, document the limitation and the follow-up owner.

Decide whether the exposed period needs investigation

An update does not explain prior access or invalidate a session that was already established. Preserve available VPN logs and identity-provider sign-in records before retention or routine cleanup removes them. Look for unexpected successful logins, unfamiliar source addresses, access through a method that should not have been allowed, new VPN users, and changes to remote-access or administrative settings.

Treat an unusual event as a lead. Compare it with maintenance windows, expected travel, account activity, and endpoint or network evidence before calling it malicious. If the evidence points to unauthorized access, follow the client’s incident-response process to scope accounts, sessions, and reachable systems. The public advisories confirm exploitation of the vulnerability; they do not attribute a particular client’s log entry to this CVE.

What I would want in the MSP ticket

For each client, the record should answer which appliance and SSL VPN configuration were checked, whether the affected path was present, which firmware was running before and after the change, how the SAML and alternate login routes were tested, what logs were reviewed, and what remains unresolved. Include the vendor advisory and the person responsible for the next step. Keep client identifiers and raw sign-in details out of the public write-up.

Across clients, a small status matrix makes gaps visible: inspected, potentially affected, updated, tested, and still under investigation. That is more useful than a single note saying all SonicWalls were checked. It also gives the next technician a way to distinguish a completed patch from a verified access path.

items.title: Showcase Review: A Movie Night Companion for the iPhone Duo
items.content_html:
One of the things I like about the iPhone Duo is that developers have a reason to think about what a phone can become in your hands. Open it, close it, prop it beside you, and there is an opportunity to give the software a different role. Showcase makes sense to me in exactly that context: a movie and TV tracker that can become a small companion to movie night.

There is some of that early iPhone spirit here: software that gives me a reason to enjoy the device as well as use it. Showcase has a practical job, and I appreciate the willingness to make the hardware part of the experience.

I also bring some history to this category. When I wrote about why Trakt is still my home base for movies and TV, years of watched episodes and ratings were central to the argument. Showcase needs to respect that record while giving me a new reason to enjoy using it.

Disclosure and scope

I received a review code. This review focuses on the iPhone Duo design, with my own device photos and researched feature, pricing, and privacy details. Performance and sync behavior have not been independently verified.

My take

Showcase’s appeal is that keeping track can be part of enjoying movies and television. The visual presentation has somewhere useful to go on the Duo, especially when the phone is sitting beside the couch. It gives the extra screens a role in the activity instead of treating them as spare space.

For someone with an established Trakt account, continuity remains the deciding practical issue. I am interested in Showcase as a more enjoyable daily interface. Before entrusting it with the whole archive, I still want to understand how its connection handles the records I already have.

A place for the Duo beside the couch

Showcase’s version 1.5.2 release notes describe an Up Next presentation on the outer screen when the Duo is in tent or kickstand mode. The queue becomes a sequence of cards that can sit beside you while you catch up.

That is an appealing answer to a real design question: what should the app do when I stop holding the phone like a conventional handset? A nearby display of what comes next suits this job. I can imagine the phone having a place in the evening, rather than being something I pick up, consult, and immediately put away.

It also gives the poster-led presentation a purpose. A watchlist is partly a practical record and partly anticipation. Seeing the next film or episode as a distinct card plays into that second part. The app can feel like a little piece of the entertainment setup.

The test for this kind of design is whether the useful action stays close. An attractive card should still make it clear what I am looking at and how to keep my place. That is where I want the playfulness to lead: an interface I enjoy opening that also makes the next decision easier.

The photos at the top show the Available queue in wide and compact layouts. The wide view fits two columns of cards; the compact view stacks them in one column.

The watchlist has a job to do

The developer’s site describes movie, season, and episode tracking alongside ratings, release alerts, discovery, and friend activity. It also lists widgets, an Apple Watch app, and the ability to snooze a title. Those features fit together around a sensible task: finding the next thing worth watching and remembering where I stopped.

Streaming availability and filters for the services I actually use make that task more practical. Siri support also offers a quick way to ask what is available tonight. I am more interested in those routes to a decision than in a longer list of titles to browse.

Snoozing is a particularly good idea. Following a show should not mean committing to think about it every week. A useful queue needs a way to acknowledge that I am interested but not ready to catch up. The same applies to alerts. A premiere reminder can help; a constant stream of entertainment notifications can become another reason to silence an app.

I would judge discovery by whether it shortens the decision. More recommendations are not automatically more useful. Recommendations from people whose taste I understand have a clearer purpose than another endless selection to browse.

Trakt support is the important part for me

Showcase advertises Trakt sync and imports from Trakt, Letterboxd, and TV Time. That gives existing users a route in. It does not, on its own, establish which fields move in each direction or what happens when two devices disagree.

I would check a small, recognizable part of my history first: an unfinished season, a rewatch, a rating, and a title I removed from my watchlist. Those are different kinds of records. Seeing the right film in a library is only the beginning of confirming that a migration preserved what mattered.

That is a practical reservation, not a finding that Showcase loses data. I have not established that. My preference is simply to keep the existing record until I know how the new app handles it. A tracker becomes much harder to replace after it holds several years of decisions.

The everyday tracking still has to work

The same release notes describe watched and followed changes that persist offline and synchronize when connectivity returns. Release countdowns now use the same local-midnight timing across the app, widgets, and Watch, and notification links open the relevant title directly. These are modest changes individually, but a tracker feels more dependable when its different surfaces agree. Showcase requires iOS or iPadOS 26.

Offline tracking also belongs in the essentials column. Recording an episode on a flight should be an ordinary action. These release notes identify improvements worth checking; they do not substitute for observing those actions on my own devices.

Pricing and privacy

Showcase is free to download, with Showcase Plus costing $1.99 a month, $9.99 a year, or $29.99 for lifetime access. Family Sharing is included for up to five family members. I would establish which features I need and where the free limits appear before choosing a plan. A lifetime option is welcome, but it only becomes good value if the app remains useful.

The privacy question I care about most is who can see my watch history. Before using the friend features or connecting another tracking service, I would check what I am sharing. Showcase’s privacy policy is there for anyone who wants the details.

Who Showcase makes sense for

Showcase belongs on the shortlist for someone who wants movies and TV together, cares about upcoming releases, and enjoys a library with some personality. On the Duo, that personality has a physical context: the phone can sit beside the couch and become part of the experience.

For an established Trakt user like me, the deciding factor is how comfortably it fits around the history already there. If that connection holds up, Showcase offers something I want more of in iPhone software: a useful tool with enough character that opening it is part of the pleasure.

items.title: Security Signal Weekly: October 31-November 6, 2026
items.content_html:
Overview

Several of this week’s most important incidents started in systems that administrators are expected to trust: a security product’s update channel, a WordPress core upgrade, a managed switch, a NAS application, and a hosting provider’s file manager. The cPGuard compromise is the sharpest example. A legitimate updater delivered code that collected root-level credentials and SSH material from thousands of servers, turning a defensive tool into a collection mechanism.

The response cannot stop at installing the newest build. WordPress and Zyxel exploitation, QNAP’s Plex2Shell reports, and the DreamHost breach all require teams to examine the exposed period and invalidate what attackers may already have taken. The same principle applies away from ordinary IT: refrigeration controllers changed physical conditions at blood-storage facilities, while patched mobile flaws were still useful against people who had not updated their phones.

Reality check: An update can close the entry point without removing persistence, restoring a stolen secret, or explaining what happened before the fix. Patch the system, then investigate the window when it was exposed.

Top 10 Security Signals

1. cPGuard’s trusted update channel delivered a credential-stealing backdoor

What happened: OpsShield says an attacker used compromised credentials to access its cPGuard update distribution infrastructure on November 2 and pushed a malicious script through versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19. The vendor advisory says the script collected sensitive server data, while BleepingComputer’s reporting says OpsShield counted 2,946 affected servers and 32 files copied from each one. The targeted material included Linux password hashes, database configuration, root shell history, SSH authorization data, and known hosts.

Why it matters: cPGuard runs on Linux web servers alongside hosting panels and is expected to help protect them. A malicious update therefore arrived through an allowed path with access to credentials that can reach databases, cloud services, other servers, and customer workloads. Installing the clean version removes the known backdoor files but cannot revoke secrets that left the machine.

Action:

  • Identify every server that ran cPGuard 5.88.12 through 5.88.19 and update it to 5.88.25 or later using the vendor’s incident guidance.
  • Rotate root and administrative passwords, database credentials, cloud secrets, and SSH keys that were present on an affected host; remove unrecognized authorized keys and review trust relationships to other systems.
  • Preserve update, shell, authentication, and network logs before cleanup, then investigate the affected server and any systems reachable with the exposed credentials instead of treating the updater fix as incident closure.

2. CISA confirms exploitation of a WordPress core upgrade flaw

What happened: WordPress 7.1.4 fixed CVE-2026-119977, a race condition in the full-package upgrade process that can expose a predictable staging path and allow remote code execution during the upgrade window. The WordPress security release urged immediate updates, and CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 3 after confirming exploitation. Wordfence subsequently reported blocking thousands of attempts, according to current reporting.

Why it matters: This is a WordPress core issue rather than a vulnerable third-party plugin, so the exposure reaches sites that may otherwise have a disciplined extension inventory. The attack condition is tied to an upgrade, which also means a completed update is not proof that the staging path was never abused while the old process was running.

Action:

  • Move every WordPress site to 7.1.4 or a later security release and verify the running core version from the site and management tooling.
  • Review web-server, PHP, file-integrity, and administrative logs around recent core upgrades for unexpected requests, new PHP files, unfamiliar administrators, scheduled tasks, or modified plugins and themes.
  • Keep management access restricted, preserve known-good backups outside the web root, and rebuild or restore a site when evidence shows code execution rather than deleting only the first suspicious file.

3. The earlier Zyxel switch patch did not stop the exploit attackers were using

What happened: Zyxel disclosed CVE-2026-107441, a pre-authentication out-of-bounds write in the GS1900 web management interface that can lead to operating-system command execution. The Zyxel advisory covers ten models. Binarly’s analysis found that the exploit remained effective on firmware previously updated for CVE-2026-7273, and researchers linked the activity to a campaign that compromised 996 switches and collected configurations and credential material.

Why it matters: A switch configuration can reveal VLANs, management paths, SNMP details, and credentials that help an attacker map or re-enter a network. The failed assumption around the earlier patch is also operationally important: a ticket showing that CVE-2026-7273 was remediated did not mean the attack path was closed.

Action:

  • Match every GS1900 switch against Zyxel’s affected-model table and install the latest fixed firmware listed for CVE-2026-107441, even if the June update was already deployed.
  • Move the web interface to an isolated management network, block internet and ordinary user-subnet access, and limit administrative sources to named hosts.
  • Review configuration exports, administrator activity, outbound connections, and unexpected reboots; rotate device, SNMP, and reused credentials when a switch may have been exposed or compromised.

4. Refrigeration attacks now threaten blood storage as well as groceries

What happened: CISA, the FBI, HHS, USDA, and DOT issued a joint warning on industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring after attackers targeted internet-accessible or unpatched controllers. The alert followed attacks that changed temperature and defrost settings in European stores. France’s national blood service also confirmed that an incident involving a refrigeration provider altered settings at three blood-storage facilities, as summarized in BleepingComputer’s report.

Why it matters: These controllers affect product safety, medical supplies, equipment life, and fire risk. A working dashboard can still present false or incomplete information if the same compromised control path can change both the equipment and its reported state. The owner of the refrigeration system may also be a facilities or service vendor rather than the IT team that monitors ordinary endpoints.

Action:

  • Inventory refrigeration and temperature-monitoring controllers with facilities teams and service providers, then remove direct internet exposure and place necessary remote access behind a secured VPN or tightly restricted gateway.
  • Change default credentials, apply vendor updates, segment controllers from business networks, and enforce safe local limits that remote commands cannot silently override.
  • Use independent temperature alarms and a documented manual response path, and treat unexplained set-point, defrost, or telemetry changes as a safety and incident-response event.

5. QNAP confirms Plex2Shell compromises and says patching alone is not enough

What happened: Plex2Shell was covered here when the four-flaw chain first became urgent; this week’s change is evidence of compromise on QNAP devices. QNAP says it received multiple reports involving Plex Media Server on customer NAS systems and now advises exposed users to assume the NAS and its content may be compromised. The QNAP security notice calls for Plex 1.43.3.10861 or later and, where compromise is possible, a clean QTS or QuTS hero reinstall plus credential resets. QNAP says its operating systems are not themselves vulnerable to the Plex flaws.

Why it matters: A NAS often holds backups, personal files, shared business data, and credentials for other services. Updating Plex closes the known vulnerability chain but does not remove payloads already installed through it. That distinction matters especially on devices that owners may treat as appliances rather than general-purpose servers.

Action:

  • Update Plex Media Server from the QNAP App Center to 1.43.3.10861 or later and verify the installed version on every NAS.
  • Disable Plex remote access and remove port 32400 forwarding where it is not needed; use a VPN rather than exposing the service directly when remote use is necessary.
  • For an exposed vulnerable system, preserve useful logs, follow QNAP’s clean-reinstall procedure, scan restored data, and reset Plex, NAS, and any reused credentials from a trusted device.

6. APT29 watering holes used patched mobile flaws without a tap

What happened: Sekoia documented a large campaign that profiled visitors to compromised or impersonated sites and then served iOS or Android exploit chains matched to the device. The researchers assess with moderate-to-high confidence that APT29 ran the operation, which also included a one-week compromise of the Plerdy analytics tracker loaded by many Ukrainian sites. The payloads targeted browser cookies, messaging databases, saved credentials, photos, location data, and Wi-Fi passwords. Every exploited flaw had already been patched before the campaign began.

Why it matters: This was zero-click exploitation in the sense that visiting a booby-trapped page was enough, but it was not a zero-day campaign. The difference is useful: organizations could block the exploit chains by keeping phones and browsers current. Stolen session cookies can still outlive a reboot and let an attacker reach cloud services without repeating the device exploit.

Action:

  • Check iOS, Android, and Chrome versions on managed mobile devices and enforce the latest supported security updates, including for users who do not routinely connect to the corporate network.
  • Prioritize high-risk users and people who visited affected regions or sites for session revocation, credential review, and mobile threat investigation when the published indicators appear in telemetry.
  • Rebooting can stop the nonpersistent payload described by Sekoia, but also revoke exposed sessions and rotate affected credentials because a reboot cannot pull stolen data back.

7. Barracuda patches a pre-authentication path to root on security appliances

What happened: Barracuda fixed CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 across Email Security Gateway, Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, WAF Control Center, Web Application Firewall, and Web Security Gateway products. The Barracuda advisory describes an authorization bypass and an operating-system command-injection flaw that can be chained for root access without prior authentication when an attacker can reach the administrative interface. Barracuda has not reported active exploitation.

Why it matters: Email, archiving, load-balancing, and web-security appliances sit near sensitive traffic and often retain credentials, certificates, message content, or administrative trust. Lack of reported exploitation lowers the incident signal, but it does not make an exposed management interface a reasonable place to wait for scanning to begin.

Action:

  • Inventory the affected Barracuda products and apply the exact hotfix or fixed firmware listed in the advisory, then verify the patch on each appliance and high-availability node.
  • Restrict administrative interfaces to isolated management networks and named administrator hosts; remove direct internet exposure and broad internal access.
  • Review administrative logs, configuration changes, new accounts, outbound connections, and appliance file changes from the exposed period, escalating to rebuild and credential rotation if root-level access is suspected.

8. DreamHost’s File Manager breach exposed FTP credentials for two months

What happened: DreamHost disclosed that an attacker exploited its web-based File Manager server between August and October 23. Affected people who logged into that service may have had FTP or SFTP usernames and passwords exposed, while a smaller set may also have had webmail session information accessed. DreamHost’s breach notification filed with California says it blocked the access, corrected the vulnerability, invalidated affected passwords, and terminated potentially exposed sessions; reporting on the notice notes that the number of affected accounts was not disclosed.

Why it matters: FTP credentials can be used to alter websites, plant redirects, steal application configuration, or stage phishing pages. Webmail sessions can expose password-reset messages and business conversations without requiring a fresh login. A provider-side reset is necessary, but customers still need to inspect what those credentials could reach during the two-month window.

Action:

  • Follow DreamHost’s notice, replace affected FTP, SFTP, and email credentials, terminate remaining sessions, and change any password reused with another provider.
  • Review hosted files, deployment history, access logs, cron jobs, redirects, and application configuration for unauthorized changes dating back to August.
  • Inspect mailbox forwarding, filters, recovery details, sent items, and password-reset activity, then rotate application secrets that may have been stored in files reachable through the hosting account.

9. LLMjacking turns stolen cloud keys into million-dollar usage bills

What happened: Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant described two criminal clusters that find exposed AI endpoints or steal cloud and model API keys, then resell the access through low-cost LLM proxy services. In the Google research, a single victim absorbed nearly $1 million in token costs, while other incidents exceeded $100,000 in a day. The actors also searched cloud environments for more credentials, created persistence, and in some cases exploited CVE-2026-40217 in LiteLLM.

Why it matters: The first visible symptom may be a billing spike rather than an endpoint alert. An unrestricted model key can become both a resale product and a path into the surrounding cloud account, especially when the same service identity can read secrets, create workloads, or disable logs. AI experiments that never entered the normal asset inventory are difficult to monitor or cap.

Action:

  • Inventory model gateways, service accounts, API keys, and self-hosted AI endpoints; patch LiteLLM and remove public access that is not explicitly required.
  • Replace long-lived keys with narrowly scoped identities, rotate exposed secrets, require phishing-resistant MFA for human administrators, and deny cloud permissions unrelated to model use.
  • Set per-project quotas, budget alerts, rate limits, and anomaly detection on inference volume, new service activation, credential checks, logging changes, and unfamiliar proxy workloads.

10. A musl edge case made some password-disabled SSH accounts usable

What happened: The newly disclosed *sshole flaw affects OpenSSH on some musl-based Linux systems when password authentication is enabled, PAM is disabled, an account has * as its password hash, and another local account has a valid hash. An oversized password can make musl’s crypt() return *, which OpenSSH then compares successfully with the supposedly disabled account’s stored value. The researcher’s technical explanation says Alpine Linux, OpenWrt, Buildroot, and Yocto configurations may be affected; glibc-based distributions such as Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora are not. OpenSSH 10.6p2 contains the fix, and no active exploitation was reported at publication time.

Why it matters: The vulnerable combination is narrower than the headline, but Alpine cloud images may include an affected alpine account with passwordless doas access. A team can believe password login is disabled for an account because the shadow entry contains *, while the interaction between OpenSSH and the C library reverses that assumption.

Action:

  • Find internet-facing and administrative SSH servers built on Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, or another musl-based system, then check PAM, PasswordAuthentication, and shadow-file conditions against the researcher’s matrix.
  • Install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or the distribution’s fixed package; where immediate patching is not possible, set PasswordAuthentication no and restart the SSH service after validating key-based access.
  • Review authentication logs for successful password logins to accounts that should be disabled, especially alpine, and investigate privilege use or new keys after any unexpected acceptance.

Closing Notes

Start with cPGuard because the known compromise involved credential collection from servers, not merely a vulnerable version. Next, treat WordPress, Zyxel, and exposed QNAP systems as investigation work as well as patch work: exploitation is confirmed or customer compromises have been reported. Cold-chain operators need the same urgency, but their response has to include facilities staff, independent temperature checks, and safe local limits.

The quieter work is still worth doing before it becomes incident response. Restrict Barracuda management access, check DreamHost-hosted files and mail rules, put real cost controls around AI services, update mobile devices, and identify the specific musl-based SSH systems that match *sshole’s narrow conditions. The useful completion note for any of these stories should record the running version, the exposure window, the evidence reviewed, and the credentials or sessions invalidated.

items.title: MoneyCoach Review: A Wallet That Opens With the iPhone Duo
items.content_html:
I would not have put a budgeting app at the top of a list of playful iPhone software. MoneyCoach’s Duo wallet is a good reason to reconsider that. A phone that folds becomes a wallet that opens, with accounts represented as cards inside. The physical action and the interface belong together.

That is the part of the iPhone Duo I want developers to explore. There was a charm to early iPhone software that made the thing on screen feel like a familiar object. MoneyCoach applies that willingness to play to an app with a serious everyday job.

I like that combination. Money management does not have to look joyless to be useful. It does, however, still need understandable totals, manageable entry, and clear choices about where financial information goes.

Disclosure and scope

I received a review code. This review focuses on the iPhone Duo design, with my own device photos and researched feature, pricing, and privacy details. No financial outcomes, bank-sync reliability, or savings have been measured for this review.

My take

The Duo wallet gives MoneyCoach an identity I can understand immediately. Opening the device and opening the wallet are the same idea. The full budgeting interface then gives the larger display a more analytical role, with room to see the account and the information behind it.

The tradeoff is complexity. More entry methods, account types, sharing options, and AI connections create more choices about both setup and data handling. I would start with the smallest useful configuration and add features when a specific need appears. A comprehensive app is valuable when it reduces work, not when it gives me more settings to maintain.

The fold is part of the wallet

MoneyCoach’s version 14 announcement describes a 3D leather wallet that opens with the Duo. Accounts appear as cards; tapping one opens the account or a transaction action, and the banknotes lead to the cash account. The developer says these are the same underlying accounts used by the full app.

That connection gives the visual metaphor substance. The wallet provides a different way to reach actual information. It makes an abstract collection of account rows into something with a recognizable arrangement.

The appeal for me is partly tactile and partly personal. A familiar object can make an app easier to approach, and a wallet is a particularly natural match for a folding phone. It has an outside and an inside. Opening it reveals things. The screen’s change in shape helps the idea make sense before I have read a feature list.

I would still want a quick route to the ordinary account view. The wallet is enjoyable when it adds an approachable way in, while the detailed tools remain available for the work that needs them.

The 14.0.1 update improves that continuity: MoneyCoach remembers whether I last used the wallet or the full interface. Wallet cards also reflect account icons and bank colors, making the presentation more useful for recognizing an account at a glance.

More room for the numbers behind the cards

The Duo product page distinguishes the Wallet experience from the full MoneyCoach interface and shows accounts and transactions together in its book layout. That is the other half of good Duo design: giving the extra space to related information.

Seeing a selected account beside its transactions can preserve context. I can keep track of what I am examining as I move through the details. For a budgeting app, that is a stronger use of a wide screen than increasing the size of a single balance.

This is why the wallet works as a reason to look at MoneyCoach, rather than the whole reason to choose it. The playful layer gets my attention. The underlying layouts need to make the financial record easier to understand.

A budget needs an understandable record behind it

MoneyCoach’s feature guide describes category budgets with adjustments, rollover, and transfers, alongside its classic budgets. It also lists Shortcuts, widgets, and Watch features. Those are sensible places to put quick actions and useful numbers, especially if they help someone record a purchase close to when it happens.

What matters to me is the relationship between the summary and the transaction underneath. If a category looks wrong, I want to find the entries that explain it. If I move money between accounts, I want the reports to reflect a transfer accurately. A chart should make the record easier to understand, not ask me to trust a total I cannot trace.

Version 14.0.1 adds customizable transaction rows, with choices such as account, description, payee, tags, and location. A preview shows the arrangement before it is saved. That is a useful kind of customization: someone checking payees may need a different view from someone separating spending by account. Reports also join the default iPhone tabs, while existing custom arrangements are retained.

The App Store listing includes CSV imports, reports, multi-currency tools, and exports. Import and export are especially important in this category. Before moving a financial history, I would try a representative sample and check dates, transfers, currencies, and categories. I would also export it again. Getting data back out is part of evaluating the app.

Bank sync depends on the bank and the region

MoneyCoach’s feature guide lists bank connections in the US and Europe, with Canadian support coming soon. I would check the in-app bank selector for my own institution before choosing a plan around automatic imports.

Automatic imports could remove a substantial amount of entry work. They also need ordinary checking. Pending and settled transactions, delayed updates, and category corrections are the practical cases I would inspect in any connected budgeting app. I have not tested MoneyCoach against my own bank for this review.

Manual entry is still a valid choice. It asks more of the person using it, but it avoids making a bank connection a prerequisite for starting. The right choice depends on whether the time saved by importing outweighs the additional connection and review work.

Pricing: free to download, then a paid plan

MoneyCoach is free to download and offers a free trial, followed by a paid subscription. There is no permanent free plan. That distinction matters when comparing it with an app that offers ongoing basic use at no charge.

Premium starts at €4.99 a month or €39.99 a year and includes unlimited accounts and budgets, partner sharing, and up to four bank logins. Premium Max starts at €7.99 a month or €59.99 a year, adding investment tools, up to eight bank logins, and optional AI-assistant connections. Prices vary by country and currency.

I would choose Premium Max only for a feature I could name and expected to use. A higher tier is not automatically a better budgeting system. For partner use, I would also check the sharing FAQ: sharing financial data and sharing a subscription are separate arrangements, and the individual accounts need the appropriate access.

A quick note on privacy

For me, the main privacy choice is whether to track finances manually or connect a bank. MoneyCoach’s privacy policy describes local storage with optional iCloud sync for manual entries. Bank sync involves external services, including AI categorization of transactions. I would be deliberate about connecting accounts and sharing financial information, while starting with only the features I need.

Where I think it fits

MoneyCoach deserves consideration from Apple users who want a fuller budgeting system and are willing to spend some time setting it up. For Duo owners, the wallet and book layouts give it a more distinctive appeal. The design makes use of both how the phone opens and what becomes possible once it is open.

I would be less quick to recommend it to someone who wants a permanently free expense log or needs a currently unsupported bank. Those needs call for a different evaluation.

The deciding question is whether MoneyCoach makes the record clearer and easier to maintain over time. The wallet cannot answer that by itself. What it does demonstrate is a direction I like: financial software can take its job seriously and still give me a reason to smile when I open my phone.

items.title: Lume Review: Turning the iPhone Duo Into a Kitchen Companion
items.content_html:
Lume is the kind of app that makes the iPhone Duo’s shape feel useful. A recipe needs room for ingredients and instructions, and a phone on a kitchen counter needs to be readable without being held all the time. Those are good reasons for a developer to think beyond a conventional portrait screen.

What I like about João Franco’s approach is that the hardware helps explain the interface. The wide layout can act like an open cookbook. Partially folded, the phone can become a small cooking station. There is personality in that idea, but it serves an ordinary task.

That is the thread I enjoy in this new group of iPhone apps. The phone gets to become something: a notebook, a tape deck, or, here, a companion on the kitchen counter. It brings back some of the fun of software that responds to the object in your hands.

Disclosure and scope

I received a review code. This review focuses on the iPhone Duo design, with my own device photos and researched feature, pricing, and privacy details. Import accuracy and cooking reliability have not been independently verified.

My take

Lume makes a strong design case for the Duo because its layouts respond to what someone is doing. Browsing a cookbook and following a cooking step call for different arrangements. The extra screen area and the fold give those arrangements a physical purpose.

The other strength is continuity. If the recipe I save can become the meal I plan and the list I shop from, there is less repeated work between those steps. That is a useful reason to choose a dedicated app over a collection of bookmarks.

My main reservation is import accuracy. A recipe manager can look orderly while quietly carrying an incorrect quantity or an incomplete instruction. I would put faithful importing and easy correction ahead of the more eye-catching features. This review does not establish Lume’s import success rate, but its recent updates make that an especially relevant part of the review.

Collecting is only the beginning

Lume’s App Store description lists website imports, folders, tags, favorites, serving adjustments, meal planning, and grocery lists. Serving changes and unit conversions update quantities throughout the recipe, which is useful when cooking for a different number of people or working with unfamiliar measurements. The free version holds ten recipes. That is enough room to evaluate a small, varied collection before paying to bring over a whole cookbook.

I would use that space deliberately. A straightforward recipe page is one case; a long recipe with separate components is another. If a sauce and a main dish both call for an ingredient, I still want to know which amount belongs to which step. The goal is to reduce copying without losing the original author’s meaning.

The version 1.0.4 release notes describe improved social-media imports using Apple Intelligence, following earlier fixes to sharing and parsing. That is useful evidence of active work. It is also a reason to compare an imported recipe with its source instead of assuming a clean-looking result is complete.

The cooking view is the feature I care about most

The press kit describes Cook Mode, detected timers, Live Activities, and Apple Watch controls. Its Duo compositions show two useful arrangements: a wide recipe view, and a partially folded cooking view with the current instruction above the ingredients and navigation controls.

The developer’s tabletop demonstration reinforces the Duo detail that makes the most sense to me: the instruction faces the person cooking, while the lower area provides the ingredients and controls. My photo above shows the separate compact landscape view, with one large instruction and the navigation buttons beside it. The screen arrangement follows the task. It gives the fold a reason to exist beyond making more content fit.

That can feel playful without becoming a novelty for its own sake. There is pleasure in opening a phone and seeing it take on a recognizable job. In Lume’s case, the useful part is having the next instruction and the quantities close together, rather than trying to remember one while navigating to the other.

The same principle applies to timers. Recognizing a time in the recipe is helpful only if I can tell which timer belongs to which task. A well-designed cooking screen should let me recover after an interruption without rereading everything from the beginning.

Lume also offers optional hands-free navigation using facial gestures. Paired with a phone resting on the counter, that has an obvious appeal when hands are messy. I would still want the ordinary buttons to remain clear. Camera-based controls need to work under the lighting, viewing angle, and movement of a real kitchen; a composition alone cannot settle that.

Planning and sharing need to survive changes

The developer’s materials describe household sharing, a weekly planner, and groceries grouped by aisle. Those are useful extensions of a recipe collection. They also introduce the questions that matter once more than one person is involved.

Plans move. Someone buys an ingredient on the way home. A recipe gets scaled after the shopping list has already been made. My standard would be whether the app makes those changes understandable without adding cleanup work. I would rather have a clear list that needs a quick edit than an automatically generated list whose quantities I cannot explain.

That is also how I would compare Lume with another recipe manager: use the same recipes and follow them through to the shopping and cooking stages. Comparing feature names alone would miss the part that matters.

Free access and Lume Pro

Lume is free for up to ten recipes. Lume Pro costs $1.99 a month, $11.99 a year, or $19.99 as a one-time purchase. It adds unlimited recipes, household sharing, scanning from the camera, files, or photos, Smart Folders, and the Discovery Feed. Family Sharing covers up to five family members. The app requires iOS or iPadOS 26.

I like having a meaningful small collection available before committing. The one-time price is appealing for someone who expects to keep a cookbook for years. I would still choose on the quality of the core workflow. Paying once does not make inaccurate imports or awkward editing easier to live with.

A quick note on privacy

Lume keeps recipes and meal plans on the device or in your own iCloud account, according to its privacy policy. The optional hands-free face controls are processed on the device too.

Who I would put it in front of

Lume looks most compelling for someone whose recipes are scattered across websites and saved posts and who wants to use that collection throughout the week. For a Duo owner, the wide cookbook and partially folded cooking view add a particularly good reason to look. They give the phone a role on the counter that feels considered.

For someone already happy with a substantial cookbook elsewhere, I would still establish that imports and corrections work before moving everything. Lume’s appeal is the combination of that practical work with an interface that makes the device enjoyable to use. The fun is in seeing the Duo become the right shape for the job.

items.title: Cassette Player Review: Bringing the Tape Deck to the iPhone Duo
items.content_html:
I miss the willingness of early iPhone apps to be a little ridiculous in a good way. The beer apps that turned the screen into a glass understood that the phone itself could be part of the fun. An app did not always have to justify its existence with another productivity promise.

Cassette Player brings some of that feeling to the iPhone Duo. Jerry Munyoka Nkongolo’s Rafikki Studio has made a digital tape deck with a clear physical identity, then given that identity room to change with the phone. The folding layout is part of what makes the idea appealing.

There is a practical reason to care, too. Music software is very good at making a collection available. I also like an interface that encourages me to choose an album and stay with it. A tape with a visible player gives that listening session a sense of place.

Disclosure and scope

I received a review code. This review focuses on the iPhone Duo design, with my own device photos and researched feature, pricing, and privacy details. Playback reliability has not been independently verified. This is Rafikki Studio’s music player.

My take

Cassette is one of the clearest examples of why I am enjoying this direction for Duo apps. It takes the physical character of the device seriously. There is a compact player when space is limited and room for the tape, circuitry, and library when the phone opens up. That is a much more interesting use of the hardware than making the same controls larger.

The main reservation is how young the app is. Its first updates address core playback behavior. That deserves acknowledgment in a review because the player has to work before its presentation can add anything. I would try the free listening experience through several complete albums before paying for customization.

The design is the reason to look

The App Store description lists Apple Music and local-file playback, animated tapes, physical-style controls, and tape customization using drawings or photos. The developer’s artwork shows the iPad player as a visible speaker and circuit board. This is software presenting itself as an object, with the mechanical details made part of the attraction.

I like that there is an identifiable design idea behind it. A transparent housing, a label, or a drawing can make the player feel like something chosen. That matters in a category where the music itself may be available through several interfaces.

There is a practical tradeoff, though. A physical metaphor can introduce ceremony where someone else wants one immediate action. The right balance depends on the listener. If I am sitting down with an album, the interaction may be part of the enjoyment. If I am trying to find one song quickly, the route through the library matters more than a convincing cassette shell.

The Duo becomes the player

The 1.0.2 release notes describe a compact cover-screen layout, an open-flat circuit-board view, an upright arrangement with the library beneath the cassette, and a half-open book layout with the two beside each other.

I like the logic of those choices. The closed phone is something portable to operate quickly. Opening it gives the player a stage. The book layout lets the collection and the currently playing object occupy different parts of the screen, so browsing does not have to displace the thing I am listening to.

That relationship between movement and software is what recalls the playful early iPhone era for me. The device changes shape and the interface makes sense of it. The interaction belongs to this particular phone.

The important restraint is keeping the music controls readable. If the tape and circuitry become so elaborate that finding a track feels like work, the metaphor has gone too far. That is the balance I want from a playful player: enough character to enjoy, with the ordinary listening actions still easy to reach.

Version 1.0.3 adds a Shelf view on the Duo, with tape cases standing in a row to flick through. Library sorting by album, artist, or recent listening and an Apple Music favorites filter provide more direct routes through the collection. I like the combination: a shelf gives browsing character, while sorting helps when I already know what I want.

I would also resist equating visual detail with audio quality. A beautifully drawn speaker tells me something about the interface. It does not tell me anything about fidelity, supported output formats, or battery use. Those would require separate evidence.

The new fast-forward and rewind effects add another part of the tape-deck illusion. The 1.0.3 update describes music speeding up or running backward over motor and tape sounds. Extra visual styles now download when selected, reducing the initial download. I have not yet listened to those new transport effects myself, but they fit the app’s interest in making playback feel physical.

Playback reliability comes first

The developer’s version history acknowledges an Apple Music playback failure in 1.0 and reports fixes in 1.0.1 and 1.0.2. Those are documented fixes, not failures I personally encountered or fixes I independently verified.

I appreciate an explicit explanation of a problem. It gives me something concrete to check. For a music app, completing an album and moving between tracks are basic expectations. I would also spend time with the screen locked and with ordinary interruptions before describing it as a dependable daily player.

That is the difference between an appealing first look and a recommendation I could make confidently after living with it. The early release history makes patience reasonable without making the app unworthy of trying.

What the purchase buys

Cassette Player is free to download and includes Apple Music playback and up to 25 local songs. Cassette Studio costs $12.99 as a one-time purchase, unlocking the full customization options and unlimited local songs. An Apple Music subscription is separate. The player requires iOS or iPadOS 26.5.

I like being able to evaluate the central activity before buying the visual extras. Someone happy with the basic player may have little reason to upgrade. Someone who enjoys making the tape their own has a more specific reason to pay. I would make that decision after confirming playback with the music I actually want to hear.

A quick note on privacy

Cassette’s privacy policy says local music and custom tape artwork stay on the device, with no advertising or analytics. Some optional extras ask for camera or microphone access, so I would enable those only when I want the feature.

Who should consider it

Cassette’s appeal is easy to understand if you miss music interfaces with physical character. On the Duo, the tape-deck metaphor gets room to become an experience you can arrange in your hands or set beside you. The paid extras are tied to personalization rather than an additional recurring subscription.

Someone mainly concerned with managing a large collection or minimizing every interaction may find less value in that presentation. For me, the reason to look is precisely that it makes room for enjoyment. The free version provides a sensible way to check playback first, and the design gives the Duo something memorable to do once the music starts.

items.title: TypeDraw Review: The iPhone Duo Becomes a Pocket Notebook
items.content_html:
Of the things a folding phone can pretend to be, a notebook might be the most immediately satisfying. A cover on the outside, pages when it opens, and room for a sentence beside a sketch. TypeDraw understands why that is a good fit for the iPhone Duo.

This is the sort of app that brings back the fun of the early iPhone for me. The old beer apps made the device into a glass you could tip. TypeDraw uses a different physical action, opening the phone, to make the object on screen feel at home in the hardware. It is a small idea with a lot of personality.

I like that the notebook is allowed to be the point. Capturing an idea does not always need a database or a system to maintain. Sometimes the invitation of a blank page is enough.

Disclosure and scope

I received a review code. This review focuses on the iPhone Duo design, with my own device photos and researched feature, pricing, and privacy details. Drawing performance, syncing, and PDF export fidelity have not been independently verified.

My take

TypeDraw’s strongest design choice is making the Duo’s fold part of the notebook. The interface has a physical explanation: a cover belongs outside and a spread belongs inside. That gives the app a sense of place before I write anything.

The newer releases make the practical case stronger, too. Separate notebooks and PDF export give that inviting page somewhere to grow. I would still check how well retrieval, syncing, and exported pages fit my own notes before treating it as a long-term archive, but organization is no longer limited to a single book.

Opening the phone is opening the notebook

TypeDraw’s listing and release history describe notebook covers, page curls, and two-page views on the Duo. The developer’s artwork carries the same idea through the paper and elastic-band details.

What appeals to me is how little explanation that needs. A two-page spread belongs on a device that opens like a book. The cover gives the closed state a role, so closing the phone can feel like putting the notebook away instead of just hiding the same interface behind a smaller screen.

That kind of design can be dismissed as decoration, but the feeling of using an app matters. If an interface makes me want to capture a thought, the pleasure has a practical effect. It does not need to make every interaction faster to be worthwhile.

There is a balance to keep. A page-turning effect should not get between me and the sentence I want to write. I want the notebook character to provide continuity, with familiar places for the page and its controls as the layout changes. The idea is strongest when the physical illusion helps me stay oriented.

The handwriting is a design choice

The developer’s description combines freely placed text and drawings with twelve handwriting typefaces and the option to create a font from your own handwriting. Version 1.8 also opens up the preinstalled iOS system fonts and expands language support. Paper and ink are customizable, with settings that can differ between books. That is an interesting middle ground: the efficiency of typed text with some of the visual character of a handwritten page.

I can see the value in that without pretending a font recreates every quality of handwriting. Typed letters remain repeatable shapes. What the idea offers is familiarity and ownership, rather than the exact movement of a pen.

For me, customization should help the page feel comfortable and readable. It should not become the work itself. I would settle on a legible combination early and see whether the notebook still feels inviting after the novelty of changing its appearance has passed.

Smart Marks and a page ready for drawing

TypeDraw’s Smart Marks follow text as its layout changes. Underlines, circles, highlights, and strikethroughs can stay attached to the words, alongside movable images and text wrapping.

Responsive annotation addresses a real tension in a digital notebook. If I underline a sentence and then edit the paragraph above it, I want the emphasis to remain attached to the words. Otherwise the freedom to draw becomes a maintenance problem every time I revise something.

That is the feature I would spend time with before making a recommendation. An attractive page is easy to demonstrate. A page that stays coherent through revisions is more useful. I have not yet measured how TypeDraw handles those edits in practice.

Version 1.8’s Ready to Draw mode keeps drawing available without a separate mode switch. There is also an option to accept drawing only from Apple Pencil, useful when fingers should navigate rather than leave marks. These are small interaction choices, but they affect how naturally writing and sketching can share a page.

Separate notebooks and a way to take pages with you

TypeDraw now supports up to five notebooks: the included book and four optional purchases. That makes room for work notes, personal writing, or a particular project without mixing everything into one sequence of pages. The shelf also carries the physical notebook idea into organization.

The 1.7 release added PDF export for one page or a whole notebook. Search and a table of contents provide routes back to existing notes, while 1.8 adds quicker book switching and settings for individual books. Those are useful foundations for a growing collection.

PDF export gives the pages a practical route out of the app. I would still try a notebook containing text, images, and annotations before relying on it for an archive. I have not independently checked export fidelity, and a PDF is not the same thing as an editable notebook in another app.

Price and privacy

TypeDraw costs $4.99 as a one-time purchase, including one notebook. The four additional notebooks cost $1.99 each; there is no subscription. It requires iOS or iPadOS 26.

Notes stay on the device, with optional iCloud sync and book locking. Those are practical choices for a personal notebook: decide whether it should follow you across devices and which books need a lock.

Who I would recommend considering it

TypeDraw is worth considering if the notebook metaphor itself appeals to you and you want a personal place for mixed text and sketches. On the Duo, it is especially easy to understand the attraction. The device and the object it represents open in the same way. The modest upfront price makes the decision relatively straightforward, provided the current organization fits your needs.

If your notes are a long-term reference system, I would put structure, retrieval, and portability first. For personal writing and sketches, though, there is something appealing about a phone becoming a little notebook. TypeDraw is a good example of the direction I want to see more developers explore: useful software that remembers the device can also be fun.

items.title: Rolling Out Conditional Access Without Creating Tomorrow's Support Queue
items.content_html:
Microsoft Entra Conditional Access can close some important identity gaps. It can also interrupt normal work quickly if an MSP enables a broad blocking rule without understanding what a tenant relies on.

A successful policy save tells you that Entra accepted the configuration. It doesn’t tell you whether someone can still sign in to their accounting app, register a replacement phone, access Teams from an approved device, or recover the tenant during an emergency.

That’s why I would treat Conditional Access as a staged change-management project rather than a collection of toggles.

Confirm licensing and decide what the policy is for

Start with one objective. Are you trying to require stronger authentication, block legacy authentication, restrict a risky sign-in method, or protect privileged access? Those are different policies with different dependencies and failure modes.

Microsoft’s Entra licensing documentation says ordinary Conditional Access requires Entra ID P1, which is included with Microsoft 365 Business Premium. Risk-based policies involving Entra ID Protection generally require P2. Other controls, including device compliance through Intune, depend on their own licensing and configuration.

Before proposing a policy, document the user population, intended resources, affected workflows, licensing, owner, and the evidence you’ll use to decide whether it is safe to enforce.

Build an inventory of the sign-ins you cannot afford to break

Start with privileged accounts, current user groups, registered authentication methods, and devices people rely on to work. Include shared or room devices, users who travel, remote staff, and applications with unusual authentication dependencies. Identify service accounts and application-only integrations separately: policies targeting interactive users do not automatically protect service principals.

This isn’t a request to exclude every complicated account from the policy. The point is to find exceptions that are necessary, justify them, and revisit them later. Broad exclusions make rollout easier in the moment but can leave the highest-value access paths unprotected.

Microsoft’s Conditional Access deployment plan recommends phased deployment, pilot groups, registered authentication methods, and deliberate exclusions before enforcement.

Protect emergency access before the pilot

Have documented emergency-access accounts that are not dependent on the exact control you are changing. Microsoft’s emergency-access guidance explains why these accounts should be excluded from blocking or restrictive Conditional Access policies and tested regularly. Monitor their use and store the recovery procedure securely.

Don’t assume an account works because it is listed in an exclusion group. Test an actual sign-in and verify that no other enforced policy makes the recovery path unusable. Different policies can combine in ways a single policy review does not reveal.

Use report-only mode to investigate, not to declare victory

Create the first policy for a small pilot group and set it to Report-only. In the Entra admin center, review the policy evaluation alongside actual sign-in events. The What If tool can help simulate assignments, but the simulation should not replace sign-ins using the real devices and applications that people depend on.

Report-only evaluates the rules without enforcing the intended restriction. It is still worth reading Microsoft’s report-only caveats: compliant-device evaluation can prompt macOS, iOS, and Android users to select a device certificate even while the grant control itself is not enforced. That is another reason to test the deployment rather than assuming report-only has no user impact.

For each pilot sign-in, compare what you intended with what the logs show. Review successful and failed events, applications, user accounts, device state, network context, and the combined effect of other policies. Some apparently successful sign-ins may hide a user workflow that still fails afterward.

Move from a pilot to enforcement with a rollback plan

When the evidence supports enforcement, enable the policy for the tested group first. Schedule the change when someone can monitor it and respond. Tell affected users what will change, how to complete a new authentication step, and whom to contact if they lose access.

Test Outlook, Teams, browser access, device enrollment, and the specific business applications that matter in that tenant. Then expand carefully. Record who approved the change, when it became active, and the expected support impact.

If a necessary workflow breaks, Microsoft documents disabling a newly enabled policy or applying a temporary narrowly scoped exclusion as rollback options. Have that decision documented before the first enforcement change, not after an outage begins. Reassess the exclusion once the cause is understood.

Give the ticket a useful completion test

A mature change record should answer more than “Conditional Access enabled.” It should show which users and resources were in scope, which exceptions remain, what sign-in and workflow tests passed, how emergency access was verified, and where the rollback plan lives.

MFA is important, but account protection also depends on the surrounding identity and application workflows. Start small enough to see the effect of each policy and expand only when the evidence supports the change.

If you’re preparing an MSP rollout, use Microsoft’s deployment guidance as the technical baseline and turn its checks into a tenant-specific test plan. A policy is useful when it actually protects access without silently breaking the work it was meant to support.

items.title: Duo Fun, Another App Project, and Cackles (Week 44, 2026)
items.content_html:
The vibe

Overall, pretty okay and chill. I had some bad neck pain toward the end of the week, which put a bit of a damper on things. Otherwise, I was having fun and feeling curious about where a few new ideas might go.

Highlights

  • 📱 I have been having fun with the iPhone Duo. After the preorder mess in last week’s notes, it has been nice to actually enjoy the phone. Trying apps, seeing what developers are doing with the extra space, and finding the little things that still need adjusting have all been part of it. My own website needed some of that attention, too. I tightened up the layouts for the Duo’s shorter views and fixed the navigation so an open menu would not get stranded after resizing. Using the site on the phone made those rough edges much easier to spot.

  • 📊 I shared Hinge Habits, my little app for tracking iPhone Duo folds. It works with Stephen Robles’ Count Duo Folds shortcut and adds daily counts, colorful widgets, and achievements, including The Foldfather. LOL. I also spent time working through Lock Screen widget ideas. There is something fun about taking a very specific new-phone habit and making a little app around it. The Hinge Habits page has more about it.

  • 📓 I started another app project. This one is a habit-and-journal app, and I am interested to see how it plays out. I have been exploring a more personal notebook feel, with artwork, themes, and a Today screen that feels like it belongs together. Getting that to work on both a regular iPhone and the Duo has been part of the process. It is still early, so I will have more to share as it takes shape.

  • 🎨 RelayByte and StylePort got some attention. I redesigned the RelayByte website with a studio video and a clearer home for the apps I am building. StylePort also reached a couple of milestones: the direct Mac release went up, and I submitted build 3 to Apple along with the optional tips. Submission is its own little milestone, even while the review process is still ahead of it.

  • 🗂️ I kept working on how I show Trayage. I updated the walkthrough on the Trayage website, wrote a guide to its smart filters, and refreshed the existing App Store featuring nomination. A lot of the work around an app happens outside the app itself: explaining what it does, showing the actual workflow, and making it easier for someone to decide whether it would help them.

  • 🔎 There was client security work in the mix, too. I reviewed an invoice PDF that endpoint protection had quarantined and compared the alert with a sandbox report for the same file. The reports did not tell the same story, so I spent time sorting out what belonged to the document and what appeared to be background Adobe activity. I kept the remaining questions open rather than treating either the detection or a clean sandbox result as the whole answer.

Worth sharing

  • Join me on Cackles! A friend built this, and it puts Clubhouse to shame! It is a live audio app for hanging out and talking with people, and it is optimized for the iPhone Duo, too. Definitely worth checking out. 🎙️
  • A Real Microsoft Sign-in Page Can Still Be Phishing: What MSPs Should Know About MadApe looks at device-code phishing and the practical questions it raises for MSPs. This was a research-based article, with a focus on what to review in Microsoft 365 rather than assuming that a familiar sign-in page makes the whole interaction safe.
  • Making My Website Fit the iPhone Duo covers the layout work I mentioned above, with screenshots of the closed phone and the open screen in both orientations. It also gets into the difference between what I can change on my site and what Safari controls.
  • How to Use Trayage’s Smart Filters to Review Your Mac Downloads walks through presets, custom rules, and checking matching files before cleanup. Finding a match is the start of a review; it does not decide whether you still need the file.
  • The Defender’s Dispatch, Issue 012: A Warning Is Not a Stop went out on Saturday. The theme was checking what a security control actually did, rather than treating a warning or a reassuring control name as proof that something was stopped.
  • On Mastodon, I boosted Stephen Robles’ post about building apps for the Duo and Apple TV. More people making things for the Duo is very much my kind of distraction right now.
  • On X, I reposted Paul Solt’s post about the skills he uses to build apps, including SwiftUI, concurrency, testing, and repeatable project workflows. Pretty relevant with all the app work I have been doing lately.

✌️ That is it for this week. I hope you have a great week and remember to be kind to each other!

items.title: LXD and MicroCloud Certificate Bypass: What Administrators Should Check Now
items.content_html:
A client certificate is supposed to prove more than an identity printed on a certificate. It is supposed to prove that the connecting client has the corresponding private key. That’s the trust boundary at the center of Canonical’s October 28 security advisory for LXD and MicroCloud.

The issue, CVE-2026-112816, lets someone who can reach the affected HTTPS API authenticate as a trusted client by supplying that client’s public certificate in a crafted certificate chain. The attacker does not need the corresponding private key. Depending on the privileges of the impersonated client, that can mean control of managed containers and virtual machines, or even root access to the host.

That is serious, but it is not a reason to declare every Ubuntu server compromised. The actual exposure depends on the deployment and what its management interface allows.

What failed in certificate authentication

LXD supports mutual TLS for remote management. In a correct client-authentication check, the server needs to associate the verified leaf certificate, whose private key the connecting client proved it possesses, with an authorized client identity.

Canonical says the vulnerable code compared certificates throughout the presented chain to its trust store. A trusted public certificate placed deeper in that chain could be accepted as the client’s identity, even though the TLS handshake did not demonstrate possession of that certificate’s private key.

That distinction matters outside LXD, too. Encryption of a connection does not establish that the application made the correct authorization decision. In this case, the TLS connection could work as designed while the identity-matching logic was wrong.

First find the systems with a reachable API

Before calling every Linux asset vulnerable, inventory installations of LXD and MicroCloud. Confirm the installed snap channel and version on each system. For installations managed with snap, start with snap list lxd and, where MicroCloud is installed, snap list microcloud.

Then check whether remote LXD management is enabled. Canonical’s LXD setup documentation explains that a default installation uses a local Unix socket rather than an exposed HTTPS listener. Where appropriate, lxc config get core.https_address shows the configured HTTPS listener address. A listener bound only to loopback is a different exposure from a management API reachable over a client network or the internet.

Ask who needs remote access, from which management workstations, and through what network controls. A management interface that is reachable only through a dedicated administrative path is easier to assess and protect than one left available to an entire office VLAN.

Do not overlook MicroCloud clusters. Canonical’s advisory identifies a path involving the public certificate of a joining cluster member. Treat cluster management and member identities as privileged infrastructure, not ordinary application traffic.

Verify the fixed version, not just the update command

Canonical lists the following fixed versions: LXD 6.10.1, 5.21.9, 5.0.11, and 4.0.15, depending on release track, plus MicroCloud 3.4.1 and 2.1.5. These were listed for the relevant snap channels on October 29, 2026.

On a snap installation, the vendor’s recommended update commands are sudo snap refresh lxd and, on MicroCloud installations, sudo snap refresh microcloud. Follow those commands with a version check. Do not assume a successful refresh means that a particular machine has reached the fixed release, especially when an update is rolling through release channels progressively.

If you maintain a mixture of older Linux images, lab hosts, and production clusters, record the release track separately for each system. The host’s Ubuntu version alone is not enough to identify its LXD snap version or exposure.

A patch closes the flaw; it does not answer the investigation

For any deployment whose vulnerable HTTPS API was reachable by untrusted systems, preserve whatever management and network logs are available for the relevant period. Review trusted client identities, recent administrative changes, instance and configuration modifications, and unexpected management connections. Scope these checks to your environment and the evidence you actually retain. An absence of logs is not evidence that no one connected.

A public client certificate is not the same as a private key, but it is still necessary to consider whether an attacker could obtain a trusted certificate and reach the listener. Don’t declare this exploited without evidence. Equally, don’t treat a patched version as proof that past management activity was legitimate.

If the evidence suggests an unauthorized connection, follow the organization’s incident-response process. Preserve affected data, review what the impersonated identity could do, and replace compromised trust relationships or credentials as needed. Avoid clearing logs or tearing down a cluster before you understand the potential impact.

The MSP takeaway

The strongest initial response is an inventory and an exposure review, followed by a verified update and a defensible check of the affected management plane. A remote management API can control far more than the machine hosting it. That makes its trust relationships as important as the software version.

Start with Canonical’s advisory and fixed-version table, identify the systems you actually manage, and document which ones need further investigation. The useful ticket note is not simply “updated LXD.” It is what was reachable, what was fixed, what was inspected, and what remains unknown.

items.title: Making My Website Fit the iPhone Duo
items.content_html:
On the iPhone Duo’s closed screen, Safari gives my site a short page with its controls running down the right side. The homepage still worked, but its welcome section took up more of that limited height than it needed to. Open the Duo in landscape and the problem changes: there is room for the full navigation, but the viewport is short again. Open it in portrait and the page has a more familiar, taller reading layout.

The image above compares all three views from my Duo. The individual captures appear alongside the changes below. They show a boundary I had to keep straight while working on the site: I can adjust what happens inside Safari’s page viewport. I cannot move Safari’s own controls with my CSS.

The viewport is the useful clue

WebKit’s Safari 27.1 notes list the Duo’s closed outer viewport at 382 × 580 CSS pixels in portrait. The open inner display is 669 × 867 in portrait and 951 × 585 in landscape. Those heights are WebKit’s small viewport height measurements, with the browser controls visible. Two windows side by side on the inner display give each page a 385 × 571 viewport.

Width alone misses the constraint. A width-only mobile breakpoint handles the closed screen’s narrow column, but it says nothing about how much vertical space the welcome block or article header consumes. Inner landscape is wide enough for my desktop navigation, yet only about as tall as the closed screen.

I used ordinary responsive CSS for this. WebKit specifically recommends designing for the available viewport rather than sniffing for a Duo user agent. The experimental Device Posture API would not have told me which of these flat layouts I was looking at anyway: it reports continuous for both fully closed and fully open positions. Its folded value is for a partially folded book or laptop pose.

What I changed on this site

The homepage is built in Eleventy, with its intro in src/pages/index.njk, the shared header and navigation in src/_layouts/base.njk, and the styles in src/assets/starter/cyberseckyle.css. I gave the existing intro, navigation, and main content areas stable class names so the short-screen rules could be targeted without changing the site’s general reading width.

Here are representative rules from the stylesheet:

@media (max-width: 42rem) and (max-height: 650px) {
  .home-intro {
    padding-block: 1rem;
    margin-bottom: 2rem;
  }

  .site-main-shell {
    padding-block: 1rem;
  }

  .post-header {
    margin-block: 1rem 1.5rem;
  }
}

@media (min-width: 48rem) and (max-height: 650px) {
  .site-header-row {
    padding-block: 0.5rem;
  }

  .site-primary-nav {
    padding-block: 0.25rem;
  }

  .site-main-shell {
    padding-block: 1rem;
  }
}

The first query tightens the homepage intro and article spacing on short, narrow views. The full rule set also reduces gaps between the topic badges and buttons.
