The second query trims the header, navigation, and article spacing on short, wider views such as the open Duo in landscape. It also reduces the desktop navigation links’ vertical padding slightly. The inner portrait view is tall enough to keep the site’s usual spacing. The rules keep all the content and links visible while spending less height on empty space.

Folding and opening the phone can also cross the breakpoint where my hamburger menu gives way to the full navigation. In src/assets/starter/main.js, I added a media-query listener that closes the mobile menu when the wider layout takes over:

const hamburger = document.getElementById('hamburger');
const primaryNav = document.getElementById('primary-nav');

if (hamburger && primaryNav) {
  window.matchMedia('(min-width: 48rem)').addEventListener('change', (event) => {
    if (!event.matches) return;
    primaryNav.classList.add('hidden');
    hamburger.classList.remove('open');
    hamburger.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
  });
}

This listener sits beside the existing click handler for the menu. The last line matters too: if the visual menu closes while the button still announces itself as expanded, the layout is only half fixed.

I checked the changes at WebKit’s viewport sizes in a desktop browser, including a menu left open during a resize, and checked for horizontal overflow. The screenshots here are from Safari on my actual Duo after the site update. Desktop viewport simulation helped catch layout behavior; it did not reproduce Safari’s right-side controls.

The strip beside Safari’s controls

On the closed screen, Safari currently keeps the webpage out of the strip behind its side controls. It fills that area with the page’s background color. WebKit says it is investigating a way to let sites use that space safely, but Safari 27.1 does not offer a settled site-side CSS switch for it.

I noticed MacStories ran into the same limit. They updated their site for the Duo’s new viewport sizes, yet their toolbar still cannot extend underneath Safari’s controls. That distinction helped me set the scope for my own update: make the content area work better now, without pretending the page controls the browser chrome.

Brim and Wider take different routes

Two third-party tools try to use that outer-screen space. They are separate from the CSS changes on this site, and the screenshots above show regular Safari without either one enabled.

Wider is a Safari extension on the App Store. Its developer says it lets pages extend beside Safari’s controls on the Duo’s outer display, with a button to switch between normal and wide mode for each site. To try it, install the app, turn it on under Settings → Apps → Safari → Extensions, then open a site in Safari and allow Wider access from the extensions menu. Reload any pages that were already open. The developer notes that some sites with fixed headers or layout limits may not expand cleanly, so the per-site toggle is useful.

Brim Browser is a separate browser, currently offered through a public TestFlight beta. Its developer describes it as using the full page width while keeping elements clear of the side camera; the current beta invitation specifically lists automatic status-bar avoidance. To install it, get Apple’s TestFlight app, open the Brim invite on your Duo, then tap Accept and Install if a compatible build and beta slot are available. It is beta software, so availability and behavior can change.

Wider changes how Safari presents a site for someone who installs the extension; Brim offers a different browser. Neither is something I can require of visitors to my website. The site’s own responsive layout still needs to read well in normal Safari.

If you want to check your own site

Start with the WebKit viewport table, then inspect your page at the closed outer size, outer landscape, both open orientations, and the narrow side-by-side window size. Look at where the first useful content appears, whether a fixed header eats the short views, whether text or buttons overflow, and what happens to an open menu when the viewport changes without a reload.

For my site, the worthwhile change was mostly spacing, plus that menu reset. A height query is useful when it solves a real squeeze; check that reduced padding still leaves links comfortable to tap, especially in a menu. The strip beside Safari’s controls remains Safari’s decision. If WebKit opens it up later, I can revisit that part with a browser-supported way to keep important content clear of the controls.

items.title: A Real Microsoft Sign-in Page Can Still Be Phishing: What MSPs Should Know About MadApe
items.content_html:
An employee receives a PDF that appears to be a shared business document. They open it, follow the link, and eventually reach a legitimate Microsoft sign-in page. They enter a code, complete authentication, and expect the document to open.

The Microsoft login page is real. The authentication may succeed. The problem is that the employee could be approving an authentication request started by an attacker.

That’s the issue behind MadApe, a Microsoft device-code phishing kit documented by Group-IB on October 29, 2026. The research is another reminder that protecting Microsoft 365 accounts involves more than checking whether MFA is enabled.

For MSPs managing multiple Microsoft 365 tenants, it also raises a practical question: do we actually know which authentication methods our clients need and which ones their environments currently allow?

What Group-IB found

Group-IB describes a phishing operation that uses business-themed PDF attachments, fake document-sharing pages, and Microsoft device-code authentication.

The initial message may resemble a SharePoint file notification or another routine business document. A link in the PDF takes the recipient through one or more intermediate pages before presenting a device code.

Instead of asking the person to enter a password on a fake Microsoft login page, the phishing site directs them to Microsoft’s legitimate device-login portal.

If the person enters the attacker-supplied code and approves the request, the attacker-controlled client can obtain access tokens when the tenant’s policies permit it.

Group-IB identified 155 root domains in the infrastructure it studied, with device-code phishing components associated with 97 of them. Those numbers describe infrastructure identified during the investigation. They are not evidence that 155 organizations or users were compromised.

The campaign is important because it abuses a legitimate authentication mechanism rather than depending entirely on a convincing imitation of Microsoft’s login page.

Why MFA can still succeed

Device-code authentication exists for a legitimate reason.

As Microsoft explains in its authentication-flows documentation, some devices cannot provide the same interactive sign-in experience as a laptop or smartphone. Shared devices, conference room systems, and certain command-line applications may ask a user to enter a code on another device to finish signing in.

The problem is that the user entering the code may not realize who initiated the request.

An attacker can start the device-code flow, obtain a code, and persuade someone else to complete the authorization. The victim may authenticate successfully, including satisfying an MFA requirement, while giving access to the attacker’s session.

That does not mean MFA has stopped working. It means the user authenticated a request they did not intend to authorize.

This is an important distinction when explaining an incident to a client. A successful MFA event doesn’t prove that the sign-in was expected or that the resulting session belongs to an authorized device.

It also explains why checking for misspelled domains isn’t enough. A legitimate Microsoft URL can be part of the malicious workflow.

What I would check in a Microsoft 365 tenant

I wouldn’t start by enabling a blocking policy without knowing what the environment depends on.

For an MSP, the first step should be discovering whether device-code authentication is being used legitimately.

Microsoft provides a way to investigate this in Entra sign-in logs.

1. Review device-code sign-in activity

In the Microsoft Entra admin center, open the sign-in logs and filter by the authentication protocol for device-code flow.

Look at which users are authenticating, the applications involved, the resources being accessed, and the available device and location context.

A device-code sign-in is not automatically malicious. But unexpected use deserves investigation, particularly when it involves an administrative account, an unfamiliar application, or an account that has no documented reason to use the flow.

The logs should help answer a basic operational question: which accounts and systems would be affected if we blocked this method?

Microsoft also documents an Original transfer method field that can help identify later activity associated with a session that previously used device-code authentication. That matters because the current sign-in event may not itself show device-code flow even when the session remains subject to an authentication-flows policy.

2. Identify legitimate dependencies

Some Microsoft Teams devices and administrative tools may rely on device-code authentication.

Before changing the policy, establish which devices actually need it, who owns them, and whether a safer supported authentication method is available.

For Teams Rooms and similar scenarios, Microsoft recommends narrowly scoped exceptions for approved device resource accounts. Its guidance also addresses excluding the Device Registration Service resource from the blocking policy so legitimate registration isn’t interrupted.

Exceptions should be documented and reviewed. Excluding a broad group of ordinary users because one device needs the method creates more access than necessary.

3. Test a Conditional Access restriction

For appropriately licensed tenants, Microsoft Entra Conditional Access provides an Authentication flows condition that can target device-code flow.

Microsoft’s recommended deployment process is to configure the blocking policy, begin in report-only mode, review its potential impact, and validate legitimate workflows before enforcing it.

I would want the change record to identify:

  • The accounts and resources in scope.
  • Any approved device-code dependencies and exceptions.
  • The reason those exceptions are needed.
  • The report-only findings and test results.
  • The emergency-access exclusions needed to prevent an administrator lockout.
  • The rollback and support plan if a legitimate workflow is interrupted.

Conditional Access requires eligible licensing, such as Microsoft Entra ID P1 or Microsoft 365 Business Premium. Licensing and existing policy configuration should be checked before recommending a deployment.

A policy should reduce the attack surface without unexpectedly taking a conference room or business application offline.

Blocking future sign-ins isn’t the entire response

There is another issue worth separating from prevention.

If an employee has already completed a malicious device-code request, blocking future device-code authentications doesn’t necessarily remove access already granted.

An investigation needs to look at the affected session, associated sign-ins, application activity, and any evidence of additional access or persistence.

Depending on the evidence, responders may need to revoke sessions, investigate newly registered authentication methods or devices, review suspicious inbox rules and application permissions, and temporarily disable the account during containment.

Microsoft’s guidance on revoking user access explains an important limitation: existing access tokens can remain usable until they expire, and application-issued sessions may require separate action.

That matters when deciding whether the account is adequately contained.

The response should follow the organization’s incident process and preserve relevant evidence. Resetting a password is useful in many account-compromise scenarios, but it should not be treated as proof that every token or application permission has been invalidated.

What this means for MSP operations

The larger lesson isn’t that administrators need another security product every time a phishing kit makes the news.

It’s that identity controls need owners, documentation, and verification.

An MSP may manage tenants with different licenses, different devices, and different business requirements. A policy that works for one customer may interrupt a legitimate process for another.

That doesn’t make a consistent security standard impossible. It means the standard needs a defined baseline and an exception process that reflects actual dependencies.

Group-IB’s MadApe research gives administrators a timely reason to revisit device-code authentication. Microsoft’s documentation already provides the mechanisms to investigate and restrict it.

I would rather establish which tenants still permit an unnecessary authentication flow now than discover that gap while investigating an account takeover.

A successful sign-in proves that authentication occurred. It doesn’t answer whether the right person authorized the right session for the right reason.

And that’s the question MSPs need to be able to investigate.

items.title: A Preorder Mess, a Sunday iPhone Duo, and Some Actual Work (Week 43, 2026)
items.content_html:
Late again. Apparently writing weekly notes on time is still a work in progress. LOL.

The vibe

Excited, frustrated, and finally relieved. I was really looking forward to the Duo, and the runaround took a lot of the fun out of it. By the weekend, I was ready to be done with the whole ordeal and just enjoy the phone. It felt good to end the week excited about it again.

Highlights

  • 📱 The Best Buy preorder turned into a mess. I had already cancelled my original AT&T preorder after finding launch-day pickup through Best Buy. On Thursday, I called the store and was told my phone was there waiting for Friday. I was excited enough to ask whether I could collect it early. By Friday morning, I was at the coffee shop, running on very little sleep and waiting for Best Buy to open. Then I learned that the store had received two Duos, both 256GB. My order was for a 512GB Night Sky model. The day ended with a delayed order, no availability date, and a warning that it could be cancelled on November 6. I wrote the full preorder and launch-day story on Saturday. That Thursday reassurance did not age well.

  • 🙌 I finally got an iPhone Duo on Sunday, October 25. I went back to looking at local AT&T stock and asked what was actually available. At one store, I was told the three Star White 256GB Duos were being held for new lines rather than upgrades. I posted about that frustration, too. To get one, I had to add a new line to my account. My plan is to transfer the phone to my existing line and then cancel the new one. Having to add a line just to buy a phone they had in stock was ridiculous. By lunchtime, I could finally post that I had a Duo. I got it through AT&T and settled for 256GB for now, with the intention of moving to 512GB when stock improves. It was not the configuration I had wanted, but after that week, actually having the phone felt like a win.

  • 🔎 Client security work sent me into browser download history. The same suspicious installer had appeared in two unrelated client environments. Antivirus quarantined it, but I still wanted to understand how it arrived. I worked on a PowerShell collector and caught a problem in my own collection logic: it was skipping browser databases that needed a closer look. After revising it, I found a matching download record. That gave me useful context without proving execution or the complete delivery route. I turned the investigation into an anonymized case study because the collection mistake and the limits of the result were worth sharing with other MSPs and defenders.

  • 🛠️ A QuickBooks backup problem took some digging. The company file passed Verify Data, but the backup still failed. Looking through QBWin.log pointed to an excessively long temporary path under nested search-index folders. Testing with a copy of the company data in a shorter location produced a successful backup to the thumb drive. One of those support jobs where the useful clue was buried in a log, and the test mattered more than another guess about the destination drive.

  • 💻 I kept working on DMGator, my Mac app project for installing apps from disk images and cleaning up afterward. This week included clearer installation screens, more useful error messages, and testing what happens with updates, damaged images, and images that do not contain an installable app. The backup and restore side got attention as well. It is still development work, but I like seeing the awkward cases get handled more clearly instead of only polishing the successful path.

  • 🚀 There was some Trayage housekeeping, too. I worked on its PeerPush listing and added the PeerPush badge to the Trayage website. Smaller bits of launch work, but they are still part of getting an app in front of people. Back here, I also fixed the site’s X large-image card setup after seeing how poorly the iPhone article preview looked when shared.

Worth sharing

  • My iPhone Duo Preorder and the Best Buy Launch-Day Shit Show is the longer version of the phone drama. I published it on Saturday, before Sunday’s pickup, so it captures where things stood when Best Buy still had no date for me.
  • Client Case Study: Tracing a Suspicious Download After Quarantine walks through the client investigation, the browser-history collection gap, and what the matching record could and could not establish. Client details are anonymized, and there is a downloadable adaptation of the collector for review and lab testing.
  • Security Signal Weekly: October 17–23, 2026 covers the week’s security stories, including PHP, ConnectWise, and Railway. The recurring question was what else an affected service or credential could reach, and what defenders still needed to check afterward.
  • The Defender’s Dispatch, Issue 011: The Vendor Fix Has a Boundary went out on Saturday. It follows that same thread into practical IT and MSP work: a vendor restoring its service does not finish every customer’s investigation and cleanup.
  • On Mastodon, I boosted 9to5Mac’s iPhone Duo review. Reading about someone else’s week with the phone while still trying to get mine was a very specific kind of temptation.
  • I also boosted Proton’s post linking its Flock camera map. The map itself lets you look up camera locations. A useful privacy-related link to have alongside all the shiny new-device chatter.
  • On X, I reposted Javi Losana’s post about Stephen Robles’ iPhone Duo app directory. The directory collects apps whose developers say they are ready for the Duo. After spending so much time trying to buy the thing, I was ready to find things to use on it.
  • I also reposted JosephZhou’s Nintendo DS take on the iPhone Duo. Given the week I was having trying to get one, an old DS standing in for the new phone was pretty good timing. LOL.

✌️ That is it for this week. I hope you have a great week and remember to be kind to each other!

items.title: GO Club Review: Why I Keep Tracking Steps and Water Together
items.content_html:
I have been using GO Club for two things I already paid attention to: my steps and how much water I drink. Apple Health records steps, and I have used apps dedicated to either activity or hydration. GO Club stays on my iPhone Duo because it puts both habits in one place. Its widgets keep the numbers visible, and I can log water from my Apple Watch without opening my phone.

That is a more convincing reason to keep an app than an attractive screenshot. GO Club has plenty of those, and Apple named it a 2025 Apple Watch App of the Year finalist. The day-to-day combination of steps, water, widgets, and a quick Watch action is what gives it a place on my devices.

My verdict

GO Club Plus works for me because checking steps and recording a drink feel like parts of the same routine. I can see both on my Home Screen, use the Watch for water, and open the full app when I want the week’s activity or hydration history. On the Duo, the wide layout makes that history visible beside today’s progress. The compact layout keeps the immediate numbers and controls in view.

There are reasons to keep other apps around. Apple Health remains the record behind the step data, Apple Fitness handles broader activity, Pedometer++ offers a deeper step-focused view, and Waterllama goes further into drinks. GO Club’s advantage for me is the pairing and how easily I can reach it. This review is based on my use of GO Club Plus for steps, water, widgets, and Watch logging, along with screenshots I took on October 26. The walking-plan discussion below is about the feature and what the screen shows; a plan card alone cannot establish how well its advice adapts over time.

Steps without digging through Health

Apple Health already counts steps from an iPhone and can gather activity from an Apple Watch and compatible apps. GO Club says it reads that motion data through Health. Its job is to make the count useful when I glance at it: today’s number and goal first, with distance, active energy, floors, and earlier days close by.

The wide Steps screenshot at the top shows how the Duo changes that view. A weekly totals column sits on the left. The daily graph, goal progress, and today’s count stay on the right. On the compact screen, the totals column drops away, but the chart and large current count remain. Both screenshots show the same 1,230 steps and 41% goal progress, taken about a minute apart.

That difference matters more than simply stretching the phone interface across a larger display. The wide screen gives me history while I check today; the compact screen keeps the check quick. The screenshots establish what each layout showed at that moment. They do not measure step accuracy or prove how smoothly the app changes size while the phone folds.

Water is a quick action, not another chart to study

Water tracking requires an action from me. GO Club cannot know when I have taken a drink, so the log control matters more than a detailed graph I might only open once a week. On my Apple Watch, I use GO Club to add water without getting out the phone. In the full iPhone view, the illustrated bottle, amount consumed, daily goal, and add control are all prominent.

The compact layout removes that separate history column. It still shows the bottle, today’s consumed amount, goal progress, and the control for adding water. The wide and compact captures both show 32 ounces consumed and 34% of my daily goal. I can see what changes with the screen size without mistaking two images for a long-term sync test.

GO Club’s privacy policy says the app can write supported entries such as water intake to Apple Health when permission is granted. That is useful if Health is where you keep the longer record. It is still worth checking which app wrote an entry before correcting a mistake, especially when you use both a phone and Watch.

The widgets and Watch are why it stays close

My Duo Home Screen has separate GO Club widgets for steps and water. They put both numbers where I already look, without requiring me to open the app to find today’s totals. The Apple Watch matters for the other half of the routine: I log water there. That combination is the best feature for me, and it explains why I use Plus even though I have other health apps installed.

Apple’s developer spotlight says the GO Club team revised its widgets and worked on a standalone Watch experience after user feedback. That account adds useful background to the product, but the reason I keep the app is less abstract: the information is visible, and I can record water from my wrist. Whether a widget updates promptly or a Watch entry reaches the phone every time is a separate reliability question from how good either screen looks.

Walking plans add another layer

GO Club’s Smart Walking Plan and Golden Hour feature go beyond showing a daily step goal. Apple’s App Store feature describes a multiday plan that considers activity, weather, and UV information when suggesting a time to walk. GO Club’s App Store listing places those tools among its premium features.

The screen shows where the idea could help: a target, a streak view, and a prompt to use location to find a walking window. It also shows the limit of what I can conclude from a screenshot. I would judge a plan by how it responds to missed days, bad weather, and changes in my schedule, not by whether the first target card looks polished. The company’s terms describe its plans as general wellness suggestions, not medical advice.

How it compares with the apps I already use

I have used Apple Health, Apple Fitness, Pedometer++, and Waterllama. Health is the underlying place for step and other health records. Fitness is built around activity rings, workouts, and trends, with steps available in its summary. I would still use those for their broader records and activity view. GO Club puts the particular steps-and-water routine I care about closer to the surface.

Pedometer++ goes deeper on steps, distance, badges, graphs, and widgets. Waterllama has a broader drink catalogue, challenges, and more detailed hydration features. If I wanted to go deep on either one alone, those are sensible choices. GO Club earns its place for the opposite reason: I do not have to treat movement and water as two unrelated app visits. The widgets and Watch logging keep the combined routine practical.

That is why I think GO Club is better for this job. It is a claim about fit, not a claim that its step charts beat Pedometer++ or its beverage tools beat Waterllama. I can keep the underlying Apple data and still prefer a different front door for my daily check.

Pricing and value

GO Club is free to download. In the US, Go Plus costs $3.99 a month or $19.99 a year.

Plus adds more widgets and customization, deeper statistics, unlimited history, enhanced goals, walking plans, and Golden Hour. The App Store lists steps, water logging, widgets, and Apple Watch support among the app’s general features. I’m using Plus, but seeing steps and water on my Duo widgets and logging a drink from my Watch are what keep me using GO Club. If those are the only things you need, try the free version first. Pay for Plus when you know you’ll use what it adds.

A privacy claim that needs context

One of GO Club’s current App Store images says “nothing is collected or shared.” The developer’s privacy policy makes a narrower statement: GO Club says it does not store collected health information on its servers. It also describes account and purchase information, Firebase Analytics and messaging, RevenueCat for subscriptions, and inputs that can leave the device to generate a walking plan. Generated plans may be saved, and plan-related endpoints receive step-completion and mood-derived progress values.

That is not evidence that GO Club misuses health data; I have not audited its network traffic. It does mean the absolute language in the marketing image does not capture the distinctions in the policy. The App Store privacy label also lists some information that may be linked to a user and other data collected without that link. Apple notes that it has not verified the developer’s disclosures. I would read the policy and choose Health, location, notification, and account permissions with that fuller picture in mind.

Who I would recommend it to

GO Club fits someone who wants steps and water together and will actually use the shortcuts around that pair: a Home Screen glance and a quick Watch log. That is why it stays on my Duo. Open it wide and I get history beside today’s number; close it and the current goal remains easy to find.

If you mainly want step analysis, Pedometer++ has a stronger claim on your attention. If you care about logging many kinds of drinks, Waterllama is the more specialized tool. Apple’s own apps remain useful for the underlying health record and broader activity. GO Club makes the most sense when those jobs can be simpler because the two habits you check most often live together.

I’m keeping GO Club for the combined steps-and-water experience I can reach from my phone and Watch. That is the part I can speak to from daily use. I would judge the walking plan after using it over time, and I would read the privacy policy rather than rely on the broad App Store artwork.
